episode.episodeDescription: One day Nick got a visit from the FBI demanding he give them data on one of his customers. They asked for it in the form of a National Security Letter or NSL. Something wasn’t right about this letter. It seemed to violate the constitution. So he set out to change the law. Learn more about Nicks work at calyxinstitute.org and phreeli.com . Check out Cindy’s book Privacy’s Defender: My Thirty-Year Fight Against Digital Surveillance (https://amzn.to/4gXuK2J). Sponsors Support for this show comes from ThreatLocker® . transcript_window.text: so I went around and I tried to convince them that this internet thing was gonna be huge and just like a paradigm -changing thing that they needed to find out about.
And I remember getting a lot of pushback from people who were like, no, that's not for us.
That's for them.
don't really want that.
And I literally just trying to get people to get email and domain names and just like put out a newsletter or put up a little web page, something.
And it was hard to convince people at the time.
It's crazy to think back then.
were not interested in spreading their message online.
But yeah, that was a time when the was very geeky and difficult to use.
And it was new to everyone.
So it made sense why people just weren't quite ready yet.
And he kept trying to sell internet access to others and finally got some customers near the end of 1994.
one of the first organizations that I got online was called the New York Civil Liberties Union, which is the New York branch of the ACLU.
And you know, were pretty prominent in New York.
You always heard about them on the news.
They were protecting people's rights, all that kind of stuff.
From there, ball kept rolling.
Word of mouth was spreading.
And Nick's ISP was gaining more more customers.
Within two years, he had outgrown his apartment and had to get a bigger place to hold all the modems and servers he needed.
Over time, it kind morphed or transitioned from like an end user access ISP to more of a hosting kind of an ISP and security consulting ISP.
And by the early 2000s, I wasn't giving individuals the internet access anymore.
I didn't have modems anymore.
had like fiber optic lines and T3 connections and I was hosting these big corporate clients.
you name a few of these corporate clients?
Yeah, had Mitsubishi Motors of America and Ikea and Snapple, Iced T.
